story: Before the blues, enslaved people in the American South sang field hollers and ring shouts. After emancipation, Black farm workers moved from slavery into sharecropping. In 1903 W.C. Handy first heard the blues at Tutwiler, Mississippi. In 1920 Mamie Smith became the first African American to record a blues song. The women who sang it on the vaudeville stage were led by Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith and Lucille Bogan. In the Mississippi Delta, singers accompanied themselves on slide guitar. Charley Patton and Son House played it before Robert Johnson. In 1923 Sylvester Weaver was the first to record slide guitar, fretting the strings with a knife blade or a bottle neck. Okeh and Paramount began recording African-American music. Blues became a genre of its own as Black families left the countryside for the cities in the 1920s. Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and Willie Dixon, all born in Mississippi, moved to Chicago. In 1948 Muddy Waters's "I Can't Be Satisfied" made Chicago a centre for electric blues. With jazz and gospel, the blues went into rhythm and blues.

story: Jazz grew out of blues, ragtime, spirituals, hymns and marches. Until 1843 Africans in New Orleans danced to drums on Sundays at Congo Square. The brass, drums and reeds of the city's marching and dance bands became the instruments of jazz. Cornetist Buddy Bolden played in New Orleans from 1895 to 1906 and left no recordings. Many early players worked in the bars and brothels of Storyville, the district around Basin Street. Bolden and Jelly Roll Morton were among them. Bolden's band is credited with the "big four", the first syncopated bass drum pattern to break from the on-the-beat march. From 1914 Creole and African-American musicians carried jazz north and west in vaudeville shows. Early in 1917 the Original Dixieland Jass Band made the first jazz recordings. The U.S. government shut Storyville the same year. Louis Armstrong started his career in Storyville. By the time Armstrong joined Fletcher Henderson's band, he was moving jazz toward arrangements and soloists. Henderson and Don Redman developed the "talking to one another" formula for hot swing. Swing big bands then took over the 1930s.

story: Most musicologists place son's earliest forms in Cuba's Oriente Province. They were made by peasants, many of Bantu origin, unlike the Afro-Cubans of the island's west. Their guitars are thought to have given rise to the tres around 1890 in Baracoa. After slavery was abolished in 1886, many freed people moved into the solares of Havana's poor neighbourhoods. In 1917 the Cuarteto Oriental recorded the first son in the Columbia catalogue. In 1920 it became the Sexteto Habanero. Around 1910 son most likely took the clave rhythm from Havana's rumba. The Habanero's guitar, tres, bongos, claves, maracas and double bass set the line-up of the son sextet. Radio arrived in 1922. Between 1925 and 1928 son moved from the margins to become perhaps Cuba's most popular music. In the late 1920s sextets became septets, with Ignacio Piñeiro's Septeto Nacional among them. In the 1940s Arsenio Rodríguez became son's most influential player. Mambo, from the later 1940s, carried many traits of son. After the Cuban Revolution, son, mambo and rumba fed into salsa, first in New York.

story: Rio's urban samba drew on rural dance traditions from across Brazil. After slavery was abolished, Black Bahians moved to Rio in growing numbers. Women from Bahia, the "Tias Baianas", founded the city's first Candomblé terreiros. Their homes held cooking and the gatherings called pagodes, where urban samba grew. Regulars at Tia Ciata's house included Sinhô, Pixinguinha, Heitor dos Prazeres, João da Baiana and Donga. "Pelo Telefone", released on 19 January 1917, was a hit at that year's Rio carnival. Donga registered it under his name, and contemporaries said he had taken a collective song. Musicians in the Estácio neighbourhood made a samba with a faster tempo and longer notes. Ismael Silva and his companions marked the beat on the surdo, making the rhythm more syncopated. To avoid police harassment, they organised themselves into what they called samba schools. Their Deixa Falar was the first carnival group to use a bateria of surdo, tamborim and cuíca. Between 1931 and 1940 samba was the most recorded genre in Brazil. Later, a new way of accompanying and singing samba, spread from Rio's South Zone, became known as bossa nova.

story: Mariachi grew out of the son jalisciense, the string music of the Jalisco area. Its early players used only guitars and harps and dressed in peasant clothes. Most sources place its birth in the town of Cocula, Jalisco, in the 19th century. Gaspar Vargas founded the group later called Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán in the late 1890s. In 1905 a hacienda family brought a mariachi from Cocula to Mexico City to play for President Porfirio Díaz. After the Mexican Revolution the haciendas let their musicians go, and groups wandered and played for a fee, which made them add waltzes and polkas. Farm workers from Jalisco who moved to the capital settled around Plaza Garibaldi. The fashion for jazz and Cuban music brought in the trumpet and pushed the violins back. Tito Guízar was the first film charro to sing mariachi, in Allá en el Rancho Grande in 1936. Silvestre Vargas and his arranger Rubén Fuentes then standardised much of the repertoire. Lola Beltrán and Lucha Villa became the first women mariachi singers. The films also made the music a symbol of ethnic pride for Mexican Americans in the United States.

story: From 1923 Don Redman's arrangements for the Fletcher Henderson Orchestra set brass and reeds answering each other. In his solos Louis Armstrong accented the second and fourth beats and ran into the main beats with lead-in notes. In the southwest, Black territory bands built dance tunes on riffs played in call and response. In Kansas City, Bennie Moten renamed his signature tune from "Moten Stomp" to "Moten Swing". In 1931 Chick Webb's orchestra began a long stay at the Savoy Ballroom. The Great Depression put Henderson's band out of business in 1934. Henderson then sold arrangements to the bandleader Benny Goodman. At the Palomar Ballroom from 21 August 1935, young white dancers took to Goodman's band. Other dance bands copied him, opening a swing era that lasted until 1946. Dancers answered with the Lindy Hop, which had started in the late 1920s. In 1937 Count Basie's orchestra brought the Kansas City riff style to the Savoy. Small bands led by Louis Jordan and Lucky Millinder played a jump swing that led to rhythm and blues. In 1940 Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and others whom swing had brought to New York began to work out bebop.

story: Hindi film song drew on Ramleela, nautanki, tamasha and the Parsi theatre. Its lyrics leaned on Urdu poetry and the ghazal. Ardeshir Irani's Alam Ara (1931), the first Indian sound film, had seven songs. It was shot at Jyoti Studios in Bombay. Its "De De Khuda Ke Naam Pe Pyaare", sung by Wazir Muhammad Khan, is counted as the first song of Hindi cinema. Irani said he had only a pump organ and a tabla player. Singers at first recorded twice, once during the shoot and again in the studio. In 1935 Raichand Boral introduced playback singing to Hindi film in Dhoop Chhaon. Its song "Main Khush Hona Chahun" was sung by a women's chorus led by Parul Ghosh. From 1934 film songs were issued on gramophone records and later played on radio. From 1948 the music director Ghulam Haider trained the singer Lata Mangeshkar. She and her sister Asha Bhosle became two of India's most prolific playback singers. Cheap cassettes carried the songs across Asia and the diaspora until that industry crashed in 2000.

story: In 1910 José Urfé added a montuno, the improvised closing section of the son, to his danzón "El bombín de Barreto". The charanga Arcaño y sus Maravillas, led by the flautist Antonio Arcaño, made popular a danzón with a new rhythm. In the mid-to-late 1930s its players said "vamos a mambear", "let's mambo", of the danzón's final improvisation. Arcaño's cellist Orestes López wrote the first danzón called "Mambo", in 1938. Dámaso Pérez Prado went to Mexico in 1949 looking for work and gave the name mambo to a new style. His band had four to five trumpets and four to five saxophones over bass, drums, congas and bongos. Each phrase ended with a deep sound from the throat. In New York the Palladium Ballroom called itself the "temple of mambo". In Cuba the violinist Enrique Jorrín of Orquesta América is credited with creating the cha-cha-chá. Seeing that dancers had trouble with heavy syncopation, he simplified it. He had the band sing in unison so the words carried. In 1951 he wrote the cha-cha-chá "La engañadora". By the 1970s mambo had been largely absorbed into salsa.

story: Chicago's established Black churches of the time discouraged clapping, stomping and improvising as unrefined. Thomas A. Dorsey moved to Chicago in 1919. From 1923 he led the band accompanying the blues shouter Ma Rainey. At the National Baptist Convention in 1930, Willie Mae Ford Smith sang his song "If You See My Savior". The convention publicly endorsed the music at that meeting, which is why 1930 is often given as the year Black gospel began. With Theodore Frye, music director of Ebenezer Baptist Church, Dorsey trained a new choir to sing his songs with a "gospel blues" sound. With Sallie Martin he set up Dorsey House of Music, the first Black-owned gospel publishing house in the United States. Apart from the words, he saw no real difference between blues and church music. Hundreds of thousands of migrants from the South, used to the blues, were coming to outnumber the church members who preferred European classical music. In 1936 members of Dorsey's junior choir became the Roberta Martin Singers. Sam Cooke of the Soul Stirrers, Ray Charles, Little Richard and James Brown went on to record both gospel and R&B.

story: During and just after the Second World War, fuel shortages and smaller audiences made large jazz bands too costly. Through the late 1940s and early 1950s, R&B players such as Fats Domino and Johnny Otis sped up their tempos. In 1951 the Cleveland disc jockey Alan Freed began playing this music on the radio and calling it "rock and roll". On April 12, 1954, Bill Haley & His Comets recorded "Rock Around the Clock". In July 1954 Elvis Presley recorded "That's All Right" at Sam Phillips' Sun Studio in Memphis. Chuck Berry, drawing on electric blues, made the electric guitar its centrepiece. Independent labels such as Atlantic, Sun and Chess recorded for audiences of their own. It was named and sold as a genre of its own once the industry saw that affluent white teenagers were listening. Haley's song, used in the opening of the film Blackboard Jungle a year after it was recorded, set the boom in motion. As interest faded in America in the late 1950s, groups in British cities such as Liverpool took it up. The Quarrymen, who became the Beatles, moved from skiffle towards rock and roll and rhythm and blues.

story: It grew from maringa, a Bakongo partner dance of the old Kingdom of Loango, related to West African highlife. In the early 1940s Radio Congo Belge in Léopoldville played records of Cuban son by Sexteto Habanero and Trio Matamoros. In August 1941 Paul Kamba formed the Victoria Brazza band in Poto-Poto. Wendo Kolosoy's "Marie-Louise", written with the guitarist Henri Bowane for the Ngoma label, sold over two million copies. In 1954, 90% of the 30,000 music requests logged by radio were for Congolese rumba. In early 1956 the Loningisa label's session players renamed themselves OK Jazz in honour of their new employer. Congolese musicians moved the piano parts, drum patterns and trumpet phrases of son onto electric guitars and saxophones. Because the imported records were often labelled "rumba", the local music took that name. Antoine Kasongo's orchestra is credited with adding the sebene, a repeated instrumental passage built on guitar figures. In the 1960s and 1970s soukous grew out of it. In the 1980s many musicians left Zaire for Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and Colombia, and for Paris, Brussels and London.

story: After the Second World War, Jamaicans bought radios and could hear rhythm and blues from the American South. Ska joined that sound to Jamaican mento and American jazz. To meet the demand, Prince Buster, Coxsone Dodd and Duke Reid set up sound systems. In the second half of 1959 Dodd and Reid began issuing their own recordings of local artists on disc. The first ska records were made at Federal Records, Studio One and WIRL in Kingston. Its rise coincided with Jamaica's independence from Britain in 1962. The producers had turned to recording local artists because new American jump blues and R&B tunes ran short in the late 1950s. Within two or three years the copied American shuffle had become ska, with the guitar chopping on the offbeat. One account credits Prince Buster, who flipped the R&B shuffle beat to stress the offbeats on guitar. Millie Small's "My Boy Lollypop" of 1964 was Jamaica's first international hit. In 1965 and 1966, as American soul grew slower and smoother, ska slowed with it into rocksteady. In the late 1970s, bands around Coventry joined ska rhythms to punk guitar in the 2 Tone style.

story: Soul grew out of African-American gospel music and rhythm and blues, joining their religious and secular styles in the 1950s. Ray Charles began a run of hits with "I Got a Woman" in 1954. Sam Cooke sang lead in the gospel group the Soul Stirrers before he moved into secular music. In Detroit, Berry Gordy founded Tamla Records, later Motown, on 12 January 1959. He turned a photography studio at 2648 West Grand Boulevard into a recording studio and office. In Memphis, the siblings Estelle and James Stewart ran Stax Records. Stax released hits by Otis Redding, Wilson Pickett and the Staple Singers. Stax put the voice further back in the mix and used horns where other records used backing singers. Motown, an African American-owned label, won white listeners as well. Between 1960 and 1969, 79 Motown songs reached the Billboard top ten. Aretha Franklin, first a gospel singer, began making secular records in 1960 and later recorded for Atlantic. After the 1967 Detroit riot, Gordy moved Motown to Los Angeles. James Brown and Sly and the Family Stone moved on into funk. Neo soul, drawing on hip-hop, grew from it around 1994.

story: In the late 1950s the slower samba-canção was the main rhythm in Brazilian music. Samba guitarists had been playing complex chord arrangements since the early 1920s. The nightclubs of Beco das Garrafas, a small dead-end alley in Copacabana, were where it took shape. On Elizeth Cardoso's album Canção do Amor Demais, João Gilberto played guitar on two songs by Tom Jobim and Vinicius de Moraes. Gilberto cut the samba drum band down to one guitar: his thumb played the surdo's part, his fingers the tamborim's. He also sang quietly, where Brazilian singers before him had used brassy, almost operatic voices. His LP Chega de Saudade, released in 1959, fixed bossa nova as a new way of playing samba. Young amateur musicians from Rio's South Zone, such as Carlos Lyra and Nara Leão, joined them. On 21 November 1962 Brazil's consulate presented bossa nova at Carnegie Hall in New York. In 1964 Gilberto, Jobim and Stan Getz released Getz/Gilberto, which won Grammy Awards. In Japan, Sadao Watanabe's 1967 album Jazz & Bossa set off a bossa nova boom. At home, MPB followed; its start is often tied to Elis Regina singing Vinicius de Moraes and Edu Lobo's "Arrastão".

story: In New Orleans, Dave Bartholomew and Professor Longhair brought Afro-Cuban instruments and the clave pattern into rhythm and blues. Longhair's way with rhythm became a basic template of funk. When Little Richard left secular music in 1957, some of his band joined James Brown and the Famous Flames. By the mid-1960s Brown put the weight on the first beat of every bar instead of the backbeat. The change began with "Out of Sight" in 1964 and "Papa's Got a Brand New Bag" in 1965. In 1990 Brown explained it: "I changed from the upbeat to the downbeat." His arranger Alfred "Pee Wee" Ellis credited drummer Clyde Stubblefield's New Orleans drumming as the basis of modern funk. With "Cold Sweat" (1967), "Mother Popcorn" (1969) and "Sex Machine" (1970), Brown dropped even the twelve-bar blues. In New Orleans the Meters had R&B hits with "Cissy Strut" in 1969. George Clinton's bands Parliament and Funkadelic mixed it with jazz and psychedelic rock. Many early disco songs and performers came straight from funk. From the late 1980s hip-hop artists sampled funk records, and James Brown is said to be hip-hop's most sampled artist.

story: The discothèque came from France: Olivier Coquelin, a French expatriate, opened Le Club in Manhattan on New Year's Eve 1960. In Philadelphia in the early 1970s, the producers Gamble and Huff gave soul lush strings, thumping basslines and sliding hi-hats. On Valentine's Day 1970 the DJ David Mancuso held the first party at his Manhattan home, later called the Loft. Gay men, often harassed in bars, could dance there together without fear of the police. Alex Rosner put the crowd at about sixty percent black and seventy percent gay. Manu Dibango's "Soul Makossa", first released in France in 1972, was taken up by New York's underground disco scene. DJs mixed one record into the next with no break, so the dancing never stopped. Tom Moulton, wanting dance songs to last longer, made the extended mix on the 12-inch record. The films Saturday Night Fever (1977) and Thank God It's Friday (1978) took it into the mainstream. In the United States it declined after Disco Demolition Night on 12 July 1979. It stayed popular in Italy and other European countries through the 1980s. Frankie Knuckles, a disco DJ, went on to help develop house music in the 1980s.

story: Reggae grew out of the ska and rocksteady of 1960s Jamaica. Many of its records were built on rocksteady rhythms, slowed enough for a doubled offbeat guitar stroke. The first reggae records came out in early 1968: "Nanny Goat" by Larry Marshall and "No More Heartaches" by the Beltones. That year the Maytals' "Do the Reggay" put the word in print. As record shops spread, producers such as Bunny Lee and Harry J could start out without a sound system or shop of their own. Rastafari shaped the songs: Burning Spear recalled musicians drawing on its emphasis on Africa. In 1968 the Kingston sound-system operator Ruddy Redwood went to Duke Reid's Treasure Isle studio to cut a dub plate. Engineer Byron Smith left the vocal out by accident, and Redwood kept the result. By 1973 these instrumental "versions", made in rival studios, had become dub. That year Lee "Scratch" Perry released Blackboard Jungle Dub, mixed with King Tubby. In South London, singers such as Carroll Thompson and Janet Kay led lovers rock. British reggae in turn fed drum and bass and dubstep.

story: In the late 1950s Fela Kuti left Lagos to study at the London School of Music. Back in Lagos he played a mix of highlife and jazz that did not sell. In 1969, on a trip to the United States, he met Sandra Smith, a singer and former Black Panther. She gave him the writings of Martin Luther King Jr., Angela Davis and, above all, Malcolm X. Kuti came to see that he had not been playing African music. He worked it out with drummer Tony Allen. The new music drew on highlife, fuji and jùjú. The name Afrobeat was meant partly to set it apart from the soul of James Brown. Kuti renamed his band Africa '70. It played a residency at his own club, the Afrika Shrine, from 1970 to 1975. story: Salsa was built on the son montuno of the Cuban bandleaders Arsenio Rodríguez, Conjunto Chappottín and Roberto Faz. In the 1950s New York danced to mambo played by Machito, Tito Puente and Mongo Santamaría. Its centre, the Palladium Ballroom, closed in 1966 after losing its liquor licence. In the late 1960s the Dominican musician Johnny Pacheco and businessman Jerry Masucci founded Fania Records. Fania brought out Willie Colón, Celia Cruz, Larry Harlow, Ray Barretto, Héctor Lavoe and Ismael Miranda. In 1968 Pacheco formed the Fania All-Stars with Louie Ramírez, Bobby Valentín and Larry Harlow. In 1970s New York the word salsa was first used to sell several styles of Latin dance music. Fania marketed it as one Puerto Rican and pan-Latin sound for people from all of Latin America. In 1971 the Fania All-Stars sold out Yankee Stadium. In the 1980s Colombia, Venezuela, Peru, Mexico and Panama made their own salsa. Its stars included Oscar D'León from Venezuela and Joe Arroyo from Colombia. In Cuba, some say a D'León performance set off the work that became timba.

story: British bands such as the Rolling Stones and the Yardbirds made blues rock by covering blues songs at faster tempos. Cream's first two albums, Fresh Cream (1966) and Disraeli Gears (1967), are counted as models for the style. In 1970 Black Sabbath released Black Sabbath, generally taken as the first heavy metal album. The band's guitarist in Birmingham, Tony Iommi, had lost the ends of two fingers in a work accident. He tuned his guitar down and leaned on power chords, which were easier to finger. The factories and metalworking of Birmingham have also been credited with the band's sound. By 1969 singer Ian Gillan and guitarist Ritchie Blackmore had taken Deep Purple the same way. Judas Priest followed with twin guitars, fast tempos and a sound without the blues. The Sounds writer Geoff Barton named the next wave the New Wave of British Heavy Metal. Its bands, among them Iron Maiden, Saxon and Def Leppard, cut back the blues further and played faster. In the early 1980s bands in the United States built thrash metal from it and hardcore punk.
